preamble: Cal has taken a bus to the coast on his own. He is walking out along a sea wall to Saltmere, a place his nan has told him about for as long as he can remember.
body:
The bus went as far as the caravan park and stopped, because after that there is nowhere to turn round. From the shelter it was two miles of sea wall, with the marsh on my left going the colour of a bruise as the afternoon got on.

I had been meaning to walk out to Saltmere for about four years. Twice I had got as far as the caravan park.

Nan calls it the chapel, although there is no chapel on the map and no name printed anywhere near it. Her mother was born out there in a row of four cottages. By the time Nan was my age there were two of them left, and now there is a step that goes down into water and a piece of wall with the shape of a window in it. That is the story I have had all my life, told slightly differently each time. Some years the sea came in one night in February and took the lot. Some years it took forty years about it, a bit at a go, and everybody watched it happen and moved their furniture up the hill.

The photograph was the reason I was out there. Nan has been at Fern Court since March and there is nothing on her wall but a calendar from the surgery, so I said I would get her a picture of the place. I could not tell you which visit I said it on. She agrees with most things now, the way you agree with the radio.

I had told Mum I was going to Ryan's.

The wall is only a bank of earth with a path worn along the top of it, and the further out you go the less anybody has bothered with it. There were sheep on the landward side and hardly any grass for them. Below me a boat lay in the mud with its ribs showing through and a gull standing on it, and further along, a half mile of posts went out into the channel in a line, black and leaning, like the last of something that used to be a bridge.

About halfway along, the wind dropped out of my ears and I could hear how much water there was. It sat behind the bank on my right, shifting itself about, higher up than the field I was walking beside. I kept going and did not look over for a while.

The birds went up twice. Both times it was because of me.

Saltmere, when I got to it, was smaller than any version of the story. The step is there. The wall is there, about as high as a wheelie bin, with an elder growing out of the top and the window-shape you can put your arm through. Somebody had been out before me and left a can in the grass. I picked it up because it seemed rude not to, and then had nowhere to put it, so I carried it round with me, which spoiled the effect.

I stood on the step. The water came up over the toe of my boot and went out again. I moved back, and a minute later it came further up, and I understood it was not going to stop doing that for me.

Nan says you can hear the bell out there when the tide turns. I stood still long enough to be sure. There is a buoy in the channel that knocks when the water moves, a flat sound with nothing musical in it, and I decided that was what she had always meant, and that she knew it.

The light was going, and the marsh behind me had gone from bruise to no colour at all. I got the phone out. I had to hold it in both hands, and even then the picture came out grey and shaken along one edge where my hand had moved. It has the elder in it and about half the window. I have not sent it to anybody. I put the phone back in my pocket and started counting the posts the other way.
